**Private Worlds**

Somewhere in a forest, a tick sits at the tip of a branch, waiting. It can't see the forest—it has no eyes. It can't hear the birds. Its entire world consists of three things: the smell of butyric acid, which mammals give off from their skin; the feeling of warmth; and the sense of touch. A tick can wait on that branch for years—over a decade, in some cases—for a single moment: a mammal passing below. Then it smells the one smell that matters, lets go, falls toward warmth, burrows in. Everything else happening in that forest—the wildflowers, the storms, the whole cathedral of light and sound—simply does not exist for the tick. It isn't ignoring these things. They are not part of its world.

The biologist Jakob von Uexküll had a word for this: *Umwelt*—the self-world, the bubble of things an animal can perceive and act on, which for that animal *is* the world.

Once you start seeing umwelten, you see them everywhere. The bee looking at a flower sees something you don't: many petals carry ultraviolet patterns, runways painted in a light that doesn't exist for us, guiding it straight to the nectar. The pit viper hunts through a sense we lack entirely—it sees heat, warm bodies glowing against the cool night. The star-nosed mole touches the world with twenty-two fleshy rays around its nostrils and can identify something as food and swallow it in about a fifth of a second, among the fastest decisions any mammal makes. Weakly electric fish swim through a field of their own making, sensing rocks and prey as distortions in their private electricity. And a spider's web isn't just a trap—it's an extended eardrum, an organ made of silk, and the spider sits at the center reading every tremor like a newspaper.

Then comes the humbling turn: we are inside a bubble too. We talk about "the world" as if we had access to the whole thing, but our senses are a thin slit in a very wide spectrum. Birds migrating overhead are feeling a magnetic field we cannot detect at all. The mice in the walls are singing elaborate songs in ultrasound we'll never hear unaided. Every dog on every street is reading an epic novel written in scent—who passed here, when, how they were feeling—while we walk the same street and smell almost nothing. The world is dense with information pouring around us, through us, unregistered.

But here's the part I love: humans are the only animal that *knows* it's in the bubble, and the only one that keeps trying to peek outside it. Every instrument we've built is a smuggled sense. The hydrophone dropped into the deep ocean that returns whale song. The telescope that gathers billion-year-old light and translates it into something our eyes can register. The seismograph that lets us feel an earthquake on the far side of the planet through the skin of the Earth itself. We can't grow new organs, so we build them.

And there's a smaller, quieter version available every day. Learn enough about anything—birdsong, wine, typography, the night sky—and your umwelt genuinely expands. The expert birder walks into a park and hears twenty conversations where the rest of us hear "birds." The world was always that rich. She just grew a new way to let it in.

Which makes me think the bubble's walls aren't fixed. They're more like a shoreline—and curiosity is the tide coming in.

- The beauty of prime numbers and the Riemann hypothesis
- How languages carve up the color spectrum differently
- The phenomenon of "sonder" — the realization that every passerby has a life as vivid as your own
- Deep time and the brief flicker of human history
- The way smell bypasses the thalamus and goes straight to emotional memory
- Urban exploration of liminal spaces
- The Voyager Golden Record
- Bioluminescence
- The library of Babel by Borges
- How maps used to have "here be dragons"

- Crow intelligence and their ability to hold grudges across generations

I think the best move is to pick something I can write about with genuine verve and curiosity — something that rewards the reader for having asked. I shouldn't write something generic like "the beauty of nature" in a bland way. I should pick something specific and let my fascination show.

Everything else that happens in that forest — the wildflowers, the storms, the whole cathedral of light and sound — simply does not exist for the tick. It's not that the tick ignores these things. They are not part of its world.

The biologist Jakob von Uexküll had a word for this: *Umwelt* — the self-world, the bubble of things an animal can perceive and act on, which for that animal *is* the world.

Once you start seeing umwelten, you see them everywhere. The bee looking at a flower sees something you don't: many petals carry ultraviolet patterns, runways painted in a light that doesn't exist for us, guiding the bee to the nectar. The pit viper hunts through a sense we lack entirely — it sees heat, watching warm bodies glow against a cooler night. The star-nosed mole, that strange-faced creature of eastern North America, touches the world with twenty-two fleshy rays around its nostrils and can decide something is food and swallow it in about a fifth of a second — among the fastest decisions any mammal makes. Weakly electric fish swim through a felt field of their own making, sensing rocks and prey as distortions in their personal electricity. A spider's web is not just a trap; it's an extended eardrum and fingertip, an organ made of silk, and the spider sits at the center reading every tremor like a newspaper.

And then the humbling turn: we are also inside a bubble. We speak of "the world" as if we had access to the whole thing, but our senses are a thin slit in a very wide spectrum. Birds migrating overhead are feeling a magnetic field we cannot detect at all. The mice in the walls are singing to each other in ultrasound, elaborate songs we'll never hear unaided. Every dog on every street is reading an epic novel written in scent — who passed here, when, how they were feeling — while we walk through the same street and smell almost nothing. The world is dense with information that pours around us, through us, unregistered.

But here's the part I love: humans are the only animal that knows it's in the bubble, and the only one that keeps trying to peek outside it. Every instrument we've built is a smuggled sense. The microphone that drops into the deep ocean and returns whale song. The telescope that gathers light a billion years old and translates it into pixels our eyes can register. The seismograph that lets us feel earthquakes on the far side of the planet through the skin of the Earth itself. We can't grow new organs, so we build them, and convert the imperceptible into the one thing our bubble accepts: something we can see, hear, touch.

And there's a smaller, quieter version of this available every day. Learn enough about anything — wine, birdsong, typography, chess, the sky — and your umwelt genuinely expands. The expert birder walks into a park and hears twenty conversations where the rest of us hear "birds." The world was always that rich; she just grew a new way to let it in.

Which makes me think the bubble's walls aren't fixed. They're more like a shoreline. And curiosity is the tide coming in.
